Action of NO, CO, H2S

Proposed mechanism of action of NO, CO, H2S. NO exerts its biological effects through both direct and indirect mechanisms. Direct effects involve the reaction of NO with molecular targets such as metal centers, DNA, and lipid radicals. Indirect effects occur when NO first reacts with reactive oxygen species (e.g., O2 or superoxide, O2−) to form reactive nitrogen oxide species. A key product, peroxynitrite (ONOO−), can modify proteins by nitrating tyrosine residues to form 3-nitrotyrosine (3-NT) or by nitrosylating cysteine residues to generate S-nitrosothiols (RSNO). Additional pathways for RSNO formation include reactions involving dinitrogen trioxide (N2O3) or dinitrosyliron complexes (DNICs), which require chelatable iron. NO also activates soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC) by binding to its heme moiety, leading to cyclic GMP generation and subsequent physiological responses such as vasorelaxation. ONOO−-mediated nitration is elevated in the SNc of PD patients, where increased 3-NT levels correlate with loss of dopaminergic neurons. In both 6-OHDA-lesioned rats and MPTP-treated non-human primates, iNOS inhibition or ONOO− scavenging reduces motor deficits and neuronal death [320]. iNOS expression in activated microglia is increased in the SNc of PD patients, sustaining a cycle of nitrosative stress and inflammation that contributes to neuronal damage [321]. CO shares mechanistic overlap with NO, particularly through its ability to bind the heme group of sGC, resulting in modest increases in cyclic GMP. Additionally, CO activates antioxidant and cytoprotective pathways via upregulation of heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) and engagement of transcription factors such as Nrf2. CO also modulates ion channels, including KATP and KCa channels, leading to membrane hyperpolarization. HO-1 increases in PD brains and in MPTP and A53T α-syn transgenic models. Low-dose CO decreases α-syn aggregation, preserves nigral dopaminergic neurons, and improves motor behavior [322]. CO-induced activation of Nrf2 limits microglial cytokine release, reducing chronic inflammation that worsens dopaminergic neuron vulnerability [322]. H2S acts primarily through post-translational modification of proteins via persulfidation (also known as S-sulfhydration), where a thiol group (-SH) on cysteine residues is converted to a persulfide (-SSH). This modification affects protein function and signaling cascades related to antioxidant defense, inflammation, and apoptosis. H2S also contributes to cellular redox balance by modulating glutathione levels and enhancing mitochondrial bioenergetics at low concentrations. Like NO and CO, H2S activates ion channels (e.g., KATP), exerts vasodilatory effects. H2S raises cGMP levels through inhibition of phosphodiesterase 5A (PDE5A) an enzyme that catabolizes it. Persulfidation of the E3 ubiquitin-ligase parkin is reduced in sporadic PD, impairing its protective activity. In MPTP-treated mice and 6-OHDA-lesioned rats, H2S donors restore parkin persulfidation, improve mitochondrial function, and rescue motor deficits [251]. Levels of the H2S-producing enzyme CSE are lower in PD tissues, which may weaken persulfidation-mediated protection and suggest a role for H2S supplementation [251]
